questions.title: How does the 'pendency' requirement for Exemption 7(A) interact with multi-year investigations involving immigration and potential terrorism charges?
questions.question_body: I am confused about the timeline in this case. The underlying immigration proceedings started in 2002, and the FOIA litigation spans many years. The appellant argued that the passage of time made the claim that proceedings were 'pending or reasonably anticipated' vague and conclusory. How exactly does the D.C. Circuit reconcile the need for current pendency with investigations that span decades? Specifically, does the fact that Farahi is an Iranian national facing terrorism-related allegations automatically extend the 'reasonably anticipated' window indefinitely, or is there a specific factual threshold the agency must meet every few years to keep Exemption 7(A) alive?

questions.title: What is the legal effect of a district court's prior finding that an agency 'seemingly' met its burden on Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: In Part IV(B), the appellate court notes that when the district court first denied summary judgment, it stated the FBI had 'seemingly' met its burden regarding pending proceedings. Later, when reviewing the updated declarations, the appellate court uses this past finding to bolster its conclusion that the new, terser Bender declaration was sufficient. Does a preliminary judicial observation like 'seemingly met its burden' create a form of collateral estoppel or at least shift the evidentiary weight significantly in subsequent motions? Or is this just a rhetorical device to say 'we already believed you once'? I'm struggling to understand how a tentative lower-court finding cures a potentially deficient affidavit.

questions.title: Can an agency satisfy segregability requirements solely through ex parte submissions without any public description of why redaction is impossible?
questions.question_body: Under FOIA, agencies must release non-exempt portions of records. Here, Farahi challenges the segregability analysis because it relies heavily on an ex parte declaration (Bender's) that he never saw and couldn't contest effectively. The court says relying on ex parte materials is 'inherent' in national security cases. But doesn't this violate due process or FOIA's transparency goals if the plaintiff cannot even argue *against* specific redactions? What specific level of detail must be provided in the *public* version of a Vaughn Index or declaration to allow a plaintiff to meaningfully challenge an agency's claim that information is 'inextricably intertwined,' especially when thousands of pages are withheld?

questions.title: Does forfeiture occur if a plaintiff fails to specifically attack an agency's document categorization scheme in FOIA litigation?
questions.question_body: In Part IV(C), Farahi objected generally that his documents were categorized too broadly but didn't explain *why* specific categories were overbroad. The court ruled he forfeited this argument under *Khine*. Is this a harsh application of waiver rules? Usually, courts require agencies to justify categories with specificity (*Gallant*). If an agency defines categories like 'Terrorism Related Intelligence,' isn't it up to them to prove those aren't overbroad? Why does the burden shift entirely to Farahi to disprove broad categories rather than staying on the FBI to define them narrowly enough for judicial review?

questions.title: How does deference differ between general law enforcement investigations and those implicating national security under Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The opinion states twice that deference is 'particularly appropriate' when national security concerns are involved (citing *Campbell* and *CNSS*). However, it also cites *Pratt* and *Clemente* regarding general law enforcement nexus tests. Practically speaking, does this mean the standard for proving an investigation exists is lower for terrorism cases than for, say, white-collar fraud? If so, what constitutes enough evidence in a terrorism case versus a non-terrorism case before a judge will accept an affidavit as non-conclusory? I want to know if there's actually two different standards being applied here.

questions.title: Is it permissible for an agency to submit conflicting or evolving declarations across multiple summary judgment motions without explaining discrepancies?
questions.question_body: The FBI submitted declarations from Hardy in 2019/2020 and then from Bender in 2023. The court acknowledges Bender's declaration was 'surprisingly terse' compared to Hardy's detailed ex parte declaration but treats them as consistent updates rather than contradictions. If Bender had said something slightly different about the status of proceedings compared to Hardy three years earlier, would that have been fatal? How do courts handle situations where agencies update declarations years later—do they look at them holistically as part of one continuous narrative, or do they scrutinize each new affidavit independently for internal consistency?
